chapter: Early recordings and arrival in New York
title: Leonard Feather, and Claude Thornhill's background in the studios
summary: Leonard Feather and others covered the scene; Claude had long worked as a studio musician and arranger.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I don't think Leonard had any --
Oh sure, Leonard was over here, because one of the very first articles that appeared on -- my contribution to the business was through the Melody Maker.

Because in those days, Leonard Feather and Timme Rosenkrantz and Mezz Mezzrow, and those guys were frequent visitors in the United States. And a lot of them will be here for an extended length of time.
Every thing is covered -- you know, the scene is covered thoroughly all over.
But I don't whether Leonard had anything to do with those or not. It seems to me that they were probably through the studio. Claude probably knew about these things.
See, because Claude goes way back too. Claude didn't have a band until after the war. But

Claude had been in the studios, he played gigs around.

In fact, there's an album -- an anthology on jazz. I imagine it has to do with the Swing era. And there are selections -- it was done at Eddie Condon's with Claude Thornhill on the piano and all that.
Yes, Claude had done a lot of things on records, you know, by his name. He didn't really have a band until -- a real band until after the war.
But he was moving in the direction that his band later took.
Well Claude was a terrific arranger! And he was arranging for Andre Kostelanetz at the time when I first met him. But he was a studio musician.
And I imagined that the studios, you know, they were in the business of making recordings too.
So they would get a group of musicians together and do a session.
